office_does: The three-member Board of Commissioners sets Kitsap County's budget and taxes, runs county property, roads and jails, and writes county land-use, building and health rules for unincorporated areas; District 3 candidates are nominated in the district and elected countywide.
race_blurb: Incumbent Katie Walters (Prefers Democratic Party), in office since 2023 and chair of Kitsap Transit, faces Kevin Tisdel (Prefers Republican Party), a former Seattle Public Utilities manager who has not held office. They split mainly on growth: Walters backs the county's urban-growth plans and affordable housing, while Tisdel wants the Growth Management Act and state density laws repealed. Both take office facing a projected $9.8 million county shortfall in 2027.

candidates.summary: One-term District 3 commissioner and former Leadership Kitsap director who chairs Kitsap Transit, running on managed growth, housing, behavioral health and transit.
highlights: Commissioner since 2023; helped complete the Comprehensive Plan update and the Silverdale Regional Center Plan [S4]
Voted with the 2-1 majority in 2025 to drop 14 rural residential rezone requests that conflicted with policies directing growth to urban areas [S6]
Wants more affordable and workforce housing; accepted a national award for the county's 75-bed low-barrier navigation shelter [S3][S9]
Pairs support for accountable law enforcement with investment in youth mental health and treatment [S3]
Endorsed by Kitsap mayors, the sheriff, the prosecutor, two tribes and the Kitsap County Democrats [S5]

experience.basis: One-term incumbent with a documented record (comprehensive plan, critical areas ordinance) and regional board chairs; not a long-tenure officeholder.

housing.basis: Prioritizes expanding affordable and workforce housing and a services-based response to homelessness, including the low-barrier navigation center; past chair of Housing Kitsap.

safety.basis: Says public safety and behavioral health go hand in hand: supports accountable law enforcement while investing in treatment and youth mental health to address problems 'before they become crises.'

spending.basis: Pledges investment in infrastructure, public safety and services alongside a 'fiscally responsible' approach and careful budgeting; no clear lean either way.

candidates.summary: Fourth-generation Kitsap native, former Seattle Public Utilities manager and collision-repair business owner, running on repealing the Growth Management Act and keeping Kitsap rural.
highlights: Wants the Growth Management Act repealed first, then the county and state density and builder's-remedy laws [S3]
Says Kitsap has a housing surplus and an affordability problem driven by King County commuters, not a shortage [S3]
Would end the multifamily property-tax exemption and opposes taxing working farms [S3]
Says land-use and infrastructure decisions must produce net-positive revenue for county taxpayers [S3]
Endorsed by the Washington Farm Bureau PAC [S2]

experience.basis: Has never held elected office and runs against 'photo-op projects', though he cites 14-15 years of utility administration in Seattle.

taxes.basis: Would end the multifamily tax exemption because it shifts taxes onto residents, and supports 'no farm taxation'; frames growth as a cost borne by taxpayers.

spending.basis: Wants every land-use and infrastructure decision to deliver measurable net-positive revenue, and criticizes ratepayer cost-sharing in the Silverdale sewer plan; he also proposes some new projects.
